source: Zhang & Norman (1994) Representations in distributed cognitive tasks
finding: Exp 1A: Tower of Hanoi isomorphs with 1, 2, 3 or 4 rules held in the head. More internal rules made the task harder, per minimum step.
numbers: 24 undergraduates, each played all 4 games. Conditions II, II3, II23, II234 had minimum 2, 4, 7, 8 steps; times, steps, errors divided by minimum steps. Main effect p<.001 on time. Order II < II3 < II234 ~ II23; II234 vs II23 not significant on time or errors.
limits: Difficulty order is not strictly monotone in rule count. Exact means are only in figures, not text. One student sample, one puzzle family.
agent_relevance: Every rule the agent must keep in its head is a cost. Write rules where they can be looked up.

source: Zhang & Norman (1994) Representations in distributed cognitive tasks
finding: Exp 1B: making the rules external (physically constrained, e.g. a cup cannot sit on a smaller one) lowered difficulty versus the same rules held internally.
numbers: Conditions II, II-E3, II-E23, II-E234. II vs II-E3 p<.01 (time); II-E23 vs II-E234 differences small (p<.03 time, p>.4 steps). Table 1 p values only.
limits: Time and error measures agree; step counts less often significant (II vs II-E3 p<.1 on steps).
agent_relevance: Constraints enforced by the medium (a validator, a schema) beat constraints the model must remember.

source: Zhang & Norman (1994) Representations in distributed cognitive tasks
finding: Exp 2: externalising more rules makes the puzzle easier, and external rules were error-proof.
numbers: 18 subjects (54 games). Order 1123 > 112-E3 ~ 11-E23 on time, steps, errors. Main effect p<.05 (time, steps), p<.005 (errors). All errors were on internal rules; none on external rules.
limits: 11-E3 vs 11-E23 not significant (errors p>.2). Replicates Kotovsky, Hayes & Simon (1985) dish-move vs peg-move on time only; here steps and errors also agree.
agent_relevance: Rule violations in the agent likely come from internal rules; moving rules into checked structure removes that error class.

source: Zhang & Norman (1994) Representations in distributed cognitive tasks
finding: Competing explanation tested inside the paper: external rules may help because they prompt a recursive strategy (move smallest object to its place first).
numbers: In the II-E23 condition 16 of 18 games moved the smallest cup first; in II23 11 of 18; in II2-E3 10 of 18. Once the small or medium object was home, 52 of 54 games finished in exactly 3 more steps.
limits: Confounds working-memory relief with strategy discovery; the paper does not separate them.
agent_relevance: A representation changes which strategy gets discovered, not only the load. Test both effects when changing the scaffold.

source: Zhang & Norman (1994) Representations in distributed cognitive tasks
finding: Exp 3: for the same formal structure, using location to carry a dimension beat size or colour.
numbers: Ordinal dimension: location better than size on time p<.01, steps p<.05, errors p<.03; location vs colour not significant (p>.17 time). Nominal dimension: location better than size and colour on time p<.003/p<.016 and errors p<.0001/p<.007; steps all not significant. No interactions significant.
limits: Size vs colour not significant. Steps rarely reach significance. Effect of internal vs external ordinal coding was not significant, authors say colour priority was trivially learned.
agent_relevance: Spatial layout (position in a grid or table) is a strong carrier for structure. Prefer position-coded layouts over labels.

source: Zhang & Wang (2009) An exploration of the relations between external representations and working memory (PLoS ONE)
finding: Direct test of the memory-aid hypothesis. External displays help only when they match how the internal copy was encoded; mismatched external plus internal info can be worse than all-internal.
numbers: Exp 1 (N=24): ANOVA on errors, representation effect F(2,44)=6.08, p<.01; error rates E-E 0.52%, E-I 5.2%, I-I 5.7% at length 2. Exp 2 (reversed encoding): length 3 errors E-E 1.1%, E-I 15.9%, I-I 20.5%; interaction F(2,40)=6.31, p<.01.
limits: Small lab task (digit comparison), student sample. Same lab as the 1994 work, so not independent.
agent_relevance: A pasted note or scratchpad can hurt if its order or format does not match how the agent will read it. Match the layout to the use.

source: Ayabe, Manalo & de Vries (2022) Problem-appropriate diagram instruction for improving math word problem solving
finding: Teaching students which diagram fits which problem type raised use and accuracy, and the gain persisted.
numbers: 67 junior-high students, multiple-baseline design. Line diagram on compare-quantities: t(66)=5.11, d=0.88. Table on predict-pattern: d=1.55. Graph on compare-trajectories: d=1.09. Phase effects eta_G^2 0.08 to 0.26.
limits: Perceived cognitive load rose first (d=0.49) and fell only later (delayed test lower than pretest, d=0.71). No control group. Japanese students only.
agent_relevance: Choose the representation per problem type, then keep it; a first-use cost is expected.

source: Bauer & Johnson-Laird (1993) How diagrams can improve reasoning (Psychological Science)
finding: Diagrams help deduction only when they make the alternative possibilities explicit. A first version with icons for inclusive vs exclusive disjunction had no effect.
numbers: Main experiment: about 35 s faster and nearly 30% more valid conclusions from diagrams than verbal premises (abstract only).
quote: The diagrams had no effect on performance.
limits: Read abstract via Crossref only. Boundary condition: a diagram that merely decorates the text did nothing.
agent_relevance: A diagram or table must expose the case split the task needs, or it adds nothing.

source: Berney & Betrancourt (2016) Does animation enhance learning? A meta-analysis
finding: Meta-analysis of animated vs static graphics. Only the title was retrieved here; no result is claimed.
numbers: Not opened. Pointer only; do not quote an effect size from this line.
limits: Not read this session. Treat as lead for follow-up.
agent_relevance: Dynamic traces (animation) are not shown here to beat static ones.

source: Hoffler & Leutner (2007) Instructional animation versus static pictures: a meta-analysis
finding: Meta-analysis on animation vs static pictures. Only the title was retrieved this session; no result is claimed.
numbers: Not opened. Pointer only.
limits: Not read this session.
agent_relevance: Lead for follow-up on static vs dynamic displays.

source: Sui et al. (2024, WSDM) Table Meets LLM: can LLMs understand structured table data?
finding: Table serialisation changes GPT-3.5 accuracy. HTML best overall, markdown and JSON lower on some tasks, differences often small.
numbers: Table 5, GPT-3.5: TabFact NL+Sep 70.26, Markdown 68.40, JSON 68.04, XML 70.00, HTML 71.33; ToTTo BLEU-4 12.70 / 8.57 / 8.82 / 8.82 / 12.30. GPT-4 with HTML: TabFact 78.40.
limits: HTML vs NL+Sep is within about 1 point on TabFact, so the text claim of a 6.76% HTML gain refers to the seven-task benchmark. Only GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 (2023).
agent_relevance: Output and input table format can move accuracy by a few points; not a large lever once the format is sane.

source: Sui et al. (2024, WSDM) Table Meets LLM
finding: Order and structural hints matter: placing the question after the table lowers accuracy; format explanations and partition marks can hurt cell lookup.
numbers: Question placed behind table: overall -6.81% across tasks. Zero-shot vs 1-shot with HTML: -30.38% overall. Best input design (HTML, format explanation, role prompt, no order change): 65.43% on 7 structure tasks.
limits: Benchmark of structure-reading tasks, not reasoning. Extra structure hint helped some tasks and hurt cell lookup.
agent_relevance: Put the question before the data. Show an example of the table format rather than only describing it.

source: He et al. (2024) Does prompt formatting have any impact on LLM performance?
finding: Re-formatting the same content (plain text, markdown, YAML, JSON) changes accuracy a lot for GPT-3.5 and less for GPT-4.
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo-16k MMLU law: JSON up 42% relative to markdown. HumanEval-X (GPT-3.5): YAML 69.8 vs plain 62.9, p<.001. Code translation varies by up to 40% for GPT-3.5. GPT-4 consistency between formats above 0.5; GPT-3.5 below 0.5, only 16% identical answers markdown vs JSON.
limits: OpenAI models only, 2023-24 versions. Best format differs by model (GPT-3.5 JSON, GPT-4 markdown); IoU of top formats across model series often below 0.2.
agent_relevance: Format effects are real but model-specific. Re-test the scaffold's data format on each model; never assume transfer.

source: Sclar et al. (2024, ICLR) How I learned to start worrying about prompt formatting (FormatSpread)
finding: Meaning-preserving changes in prompt format (separators, casing) swing open-source LLM accuracy a lot. Sensitivity persists with larger models, more shots, and instruction tuning.
numbers: Up to 76 accuracy points difference on LLaMA-2-13B across plausible formats. Format ranking only weakly correlated between models.
limits: Few-shot, open models of 2023. Notation-level changes, not diagrams.
agent_relevance: Report a range across formats when judging the scaffold; a single format can mislead a comparison by tens of points.

source: Fatemi, Halcrow & Perozzi (2023) Talk like a graph: encoding graphs for LLMs
finding: How a graph is written as text strongly changes accuracy, task by task. Incident-list encoding beats adjacency-list for finding connected nodes.
numbers: Connected nodes (PaLM 62B): adjacency 19.8%, incident 53.8%. Choice of encoder gives gains from 4.8% to 61.8% depending on task. Integer node names help integer-output tasks; names like David help edge-existence and cycle check.
quote: encoding the graph structure in a way that makes the relevant information more accessible
limits: One model family (PaLM 2); synthetic graphs; no single best encoding across tasks. Closest LLM echo of Larkin and Simon: same data, different index, different ease.
agent_relevance: Store linked state so each query reads the needed items next to each other (incident list), not scattered (adjacency).

source: Wang et al. (2023) Can language models solve graph problems in natural language? (NLGraph)
finding: LLMs solve simple graph tasks from text, but prompting tricks fail on harder ones, and special structures hurt.
numbers: 29,370 problems, 8 tasks. LLMs 37.33% to 57.82% above random on connectivity, cycle, shortest path. Chain-of-thought, least-to-most and self-consistency helped on simple tasks only; on hard tasks few-shot in-context learning did not improve. Build-a-Graph prompting gave +3.07% to +16.85%.
limits: Text-only representation; nobody tested a drawn or spatial one. Chain and clique connectivity cases were much worse than average.
agent_relevance: Linear text traces are weak for global structure; give the agent an explicit structured scratch state for graphs.

source: Wu et al. (2024, NeurIPS) Mind's eye of LLMs: Visualization-of-Thought
finding: Asking the model to draw its own state in text-grid form after each step improves spatial reasoning over plain chain of thought, and over GPT-4V seeing images.
numbers: Natural-language navigation, GPT-4: VoT 59.00, CoT 54.00, no-visualisation 35.50 (VoT +23.5 over no-viz; p<0.16 vs CoT). Visual state tracking rates: VoT 87-99%, CoT 57-59% depending on task. Accurate state drawings only 24-26% of the time; with accurate drawings, correct decisions 65-77%.
limits: Gain over CoT in the language task not significant at 0.05. In a ring navigation task, CoT 52.5% beat VoT 49.5% (200 items): when the task reduces to arithmetic, drawing does not help. Visualisations are often wrong. Wording of prompt matters.
agent_relevance: A drawn state helps only on tasks that are spatial; verify the drawing itself. Do not apply to arithmetic-like steps.

source: Menon et al. (2024) Whiteboard-of-Thought
finding: Letting a multimodal model draw with code and read its own picture lifts accuracy where text reasoning fails, and hurts where text coordinates already work.
numbers: ASCII understanding: up to 92% with WoT where baselines get 0% on some instances; text-only fails every truly visual ASCII instance. Navigation overall: Direct 33, CoT 42, WoT 52. Hexagon: CoT 8% to WoT 61%. Square grid: CoT 98% vs WoT 50%.
limits: Perception errors in the model's own drawing dominate failures. Square-grid result is a clear boundary: text coordinates beat drawings when the grid is easy to write as numbers.
agent_relevance: Use a drawn or tabular scratchpad only when the geometry is awkward in text. Check the output with a second reading.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Visual Sketchpad
finding: Giving a model tools to sketch lines, plots and auxiliary constructions raises math and vision scores.
numbers: Averages: +11.2% for GPT-4o and +23.4% for GPT-4 Turbo on math tasks; GPT-4o max-flow 66.3% (+41.3 points); vision tasks +9.0% (BLINK, GPT-4o) and +14.3% on V*Bench. Convexity and parity over 88% (GPT-4o).
limits: Gain depends on the model reading the generated sketch: relative depth gained 12.1% for GPT-4o but only 2.4% for GPT-4 Turbo.
agent_relevance: An external drawing helps only if the reader can parse it. The agent should check that its own diagrams are readable.

source: Li et al. (2025) Imagine while reasoning in space: multimodal visualization-of-thought (MVoT)
finding: Interleaving generated images with text thoughts is more robust than text-only chain of thought when the world gets complex.
numbers: FrozenLake: MVoT 85.60%, better than Direct and CoT; CoT fell below Direct there, with 90.80% of its errors from wrong textual coordinates of holes. MAZE: MVoT 92.95% vs CoT over 95%; MiniBehavior: MVoT 95.14%, CoT over 95%.
limits: On simple grids text coordinates win. Image generation is trained into one model, not a general tool.
agent_relevance: Text state works for sparse states and breaks when many entities must be placed; use richer structure only then.

source: Rahmanzadehgervi et al. (2025) Vision language models are blind (BlindTest)
finding: Strong vision-language models fail simple diagram questions that humans answer perfectly when shapes touch or are close.
numbers: Four VLMs average 58.07% on 7 simple tasks (line crossings, circle overlap, circled letter, counting circles); best Sonnet 3.5 at 77.84%; human expected 100%. Near 100% when shapes are spaced apart.
limits: Probing shows the encoder holds the information; the language side fails to decode it. Newer models not measured here.
agent_relevance: Do not trust the agent's reading of an image diagram for fine detail. Prefer structured data over pictures.

source: Lawsen (2025) A comment on Shojaee et al. (The Illusion of the Illusion of Thinking)
finding: Re-analysis: the reported collapse on Tower of Hanoi comes from the output format. Asking for a short generating function instead of a full move list removes the failure.
numbers: Move lists exceed output limits at larger disk counts; models stated they would stop to save space. Preliminary runs with function output show high accuracy on instances previously scored zero. River-crossing set had impossible instances for N>=6.
limits: Preliminary runs, no reported counts in the comment. An unreviewed note.
agent_relevance: The answer's notation (a compact program versus an exhaustive list) decides success. Ask for the compact form.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The illusion of thinking (Apple)
finding: Reasoning models fall to zero accuracy at higher complexity on Tower of Hanoi and other puzzles, even when handed the solving algorithm.
numbers: Figure 8: giving the Tower of Hanoi algorithm in the prompt did not move the collapse point. Models cut reasoning effort near collapse. Hanoi tested at N=10 with over 100 moves.
limits: Disputed by Lawsen (token limits, impossible instances). Tests move-list output only.
agent_relevance: Pair with the Lawsen line: format of output confounds the claim. Do not use as proof of a reasoning limit.

source: Lampinen et al. (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: LMs, like people, reason better when content fits the logic. Same logical form, different surface content gives different accuracy (the isomorph effect, in LLMs).
numbers: Abstract only: three tasks (NLI, syllogisms, Wason selection), models and humans show matching patterns.
limits: Only the abstract was read this session. Counts not extracted.
agent_relevance: Surface form of the same problem changes answers; check the scaffold with isomorphic rewrites.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Reasoning or reciting? Counterfactual tasks
finding: Models do worse on counterfactual variants of familiar tasks (for example other number bases), suggesting partial reliance on familiar formats.
numbers: Not extracted; only the paper's first page was seen.
limits: Not read in detail.
agent_relevance: A scaffold that works on standard notation may not transfer to unusual notation.

source: Kotovsky, Hayes & Simon (1985) Why are some problems hard? (via Zhang & Norman 1994)
finding: Earlier finding that isomorphs of Tower of Hanoi differ strongly in difficulty depending on rules being perceptually available. Known here only through Zhang and Norman's description.
numbers: Second-hand: reported solution times only; Zhang and Norman's step and error counts matched the time ordering.
limits: Not opened directly. Hayes and Simon (1977) reported isomorph differences before.
agent_relevance: Backs the claim that the same logic in a different form is a different problem.

source: Larkin & Simon (1987) Why a diagram is (sometimes) worth ten thousand words
finding: Founding claim: diagrams help by indexing information by location, which cuts search and eases recognition. Not opened this session (publisher page blocked).
numbers: No numbers; computational model of search and recognition, with pulley and geometry examples.
limits: Cited by Zhang and Wang (2009) as the challenge to the pure memory-aid view. Zhang and Wang in turn show coordination, not storage, decides the benefit.
agent_relevance: Index by location: related facts should sit next to each other in the scaffold state.

source: Zhang & Wang (2009) PLoS ONE (discussion of Larkin & Simon challenge)
finding: Positions the memory-aid view as challenged by Larkin and Simon, and cites the older list-mixing results: one list in memory plus one on screen is slower and more error-prone than both in one place.
numbers: Weber, Burt & Noll list-mixing task, as reported: mixed internal-external slower and more error-prone than all-internal or all-external.
limits: Second-hand description of older studies.
agent_relevance: Splitting the same information between memory and notes costs coordination; keep each task's inputs in one place.
